lease1-ye-know-the-heart-of-a-stranger.reason: Builds the stranger's position and Exodus/Deuteronomy first; the plain answer (what you know and they need, you tell) arrives only in the last paragraph.
lease1-ye-know-the-heart-of-a-stranger.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. What do you owe a tenant who does not know the building, down to where the water shutoff is? You owe them what you know and they need. A tenant stands where Scripture puts the stranger, and you were once a stranger too (Exodus 23:9). So you tell them plainly, the way Yahweh loves the stranger with real provision (Deuteronomy 10:18).
lease1-ye-know-the-heart-of-a-stranger.example: THE FIRST WEEK. Say a family moves in during November. Before they ask, you tell them where the shutoff valve is, what the heat really cost the last tenant in January, the midnight number that actually answers, and which repair is already scheduled. None of it costs you the building. All of it keeps them from learning the hard way.
lease1-ye-know-the-heart-of-a-stranger.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. What do you owe the stranger who does not know the water shutoff? Everything you know that they need: the shutoff, the real winter cost, who answers at midnight, what repair is scheduled and what is not. The gap between what you know and what they know is not an advantage to manage. It is the stranger's position, and you know that heart from the inside. Telling them is how you imitate your Father, who loves the stranger with food and raiment (Deuteronomy 10:18-19).

teen.open: What do you owe a new tenant who doesn't know the building? You tell them what you know that they need.
teen.close: So tell them where the shutoff is, what heat costs, and who to call at midnight. You know how it feels to be the new one, so treat them the way you'd want to be treated.

senior.open: The title asks what a landlord owes a tenant who cannot yet see the building. The Word's answer is simple: what you know and they need, you tell them.
senior.close: So the debt is information shared freely. You remember being the stranger, and Yahweh loves the stranger with real provision, so you close the gap rather than profit from it (Deuteronomy 10:18-19).

lease3-hear-it-before-you-answer-it.reason: Proverbs 18:17 answers the why in the first third (the first story seems just because it is uncontested); applies it to screening, disputes and arrears; ends on a pastoral caution rather than the answer.
lease3-hear-it-before-you-answer-it.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Why does every tenant decision need a second hearing? Because the first story always sounds right, even when the person telling it is honest. It is uncontested, and your mind fills in the gaps in its favour (Proverbs 18:17). Deciding on one account risks both folly and shame (Proverbs 18:13), so the remedy is to search out the other side before you answer.
lease3-hear-it-before-you-answer-it.example: TWO DOORS ON ONE HALLWAY. Say the tenant in 2A calls first about noise from 2B, and the account is calm and believable. Before any notice or fee, you knock on 2B. You learn a new baby is up at night and the family did not know the walls carry sound. The first story was honest. It was also half of one.
lease3-hear-it-before-you-answer-it.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Why does every tenant decision need a second hearing? Because one account is structurally incomplete. The applicant's explanation, the first caller in a dispute, and the arrears ledger can each be true and still be missing the other half. So call the prior landlord, hear the other household in a way they can tell was a hearing, and ask what the ledger cannot know. That is not distrust of people. It is refusing to decide about a household on half the information, the same hearing you would want for yourself.

teen.open: Why hear both sides before deciding? Because the first story always sounds right, even when it is only half the story.
teen.close: So before you decide anything about someone, go hear the other side. It's not about distrust. It's about not judging on half the facts.

senior.open: The title asks why a second hearing is needed. Scripture's answer is that the first account seems just simply because no one has yet searched it (Proverbs 18:17).
senior.close: So every decision about a household waits for the second account: the prior landlord, the other unit, the story behind the ledger. That is the same fairness each of us would want extended to us.

lease2-the-gold-ring-and-the-vile-raimen.reason: James 2 scene and verdict come first; the plain answer (seat by written criteria set before the showing, and write down your appearance reactions) arrives late; ends on a protected-class aside.
lease2-the-gold-ring-and-the-vile-raimen.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Who gets the good seat? The applicant who meets criteria you wrote down before the showing, not the one who looks impressive. James calls sizing people up by appearance partiality and sin (James 2:2-9), and it hides because it feels like good judgment. Yahweh's standard is to hear the small as well as the great (Deuteronomy 1:17).
lease2-the-gold-ring-and-the-vile-raimen.example: AFTER THE SHOWING. Say two applicants view the unit. You score both against your list: income against rent, payment history, references actually called, the prior landlord verified, occupancy for the unit. Then you write a second list of what was not on the first: one arrived in a new car, one brought three children and spoke with an accent. That second list is where you see your own partiality.
lease2-the-gold-ring-and-the-vile-raimen.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Who gets the good seat? The applicant your written criteria choose, ranked in order before anyone walked in. An assessment formed from clothes, cars or accents is complete before a single fact arrives, and James names it sin (James 2:9). Written criteria will not make you impartial on their own, but writing down every reaction that was not on the list makes your partiality visible to you, and that is where repentance starts. You hold a delegated office, because the judgment is Yahweh's (Deuteronomy 1:17).

teen.open: Who gets the good seat? Not the one who looks the richest. The one who meets the rules you set before they walked in.
teen.close: So write your rules down first, then notice when you're judging by clothes or looks. Seeing that in yourself is how you fix it.

senior.open: The title asks how a quick judgment about appearance can decide a rental. James shows it happens before a single fact arrives, and calls it partiality (James 2:4).
senior.close: So the good seat goes to the applicant your written criteria select, set in order before the showing. Recording your other reactions makes partiality visible, and the judgment remains Yahweh's (Deuteronomy 1:17).

lease4-read-the-covenant-in-their-hearin.reason: Exodus 24 pattern comes first; the plain answer (a signature shows assent but not understanding, so read the five key clauses aloud and have them restated) arrives in the middle.
lease4-read-the-covenant-in-their-hearin.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Did you really agree to that lease? Maybe not. A signature shows you assented. It does not show you understood. At Sinai the terms were read aloud and the people answered afterward in their own words (Exodus 24:3-7). So read the clauses most likely to surprise, aloud, and ask the tenant to say them back.
lease4-read-the-covenant-in-their-hearin.example: ONE MINUTE AT THE TABLE. Say you read the late fee clause aloud and ask the tenant to say it back. They say rent is late after the fifth. The lease says the third. You have just found a clause your document said badly, for the price of one minute instead of a dispute eight months from now. You note the date and that all five clauses were restated.
lease4-read-the-covenant-in-their-hearin.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Did you really agree to that lease? You did only if you heard the terms and could say them back. So read the five clauses that surprise people later, aloud: notice to vacate, the late fee, the deposit, the repair split, and the sharpest rules. Ask for each in the tenant's own words, and accept no nod. Then write a dated note of the reading. That note shows the hearing, not just the pen, which is what Exodus 24:7 recorded: read in their audience, and answered.

teen.open: Did you really agree to that lease if nobody read it to you? Signing shows you said yes, not that you understood.
teen.close: So read the big parts out loud and have the tenant say them back. Then the yes actually means something.

senior.open: The title asks whether a signature proves agreement. It proves assent, not understanding, and the covenant at Sinai was read aloud before the people answered (Exodus 24:7).
senior.close: So a lease is truly agreed when its key clauses are read aloud, restated by the tenant, and the reading is recorded. That evidences the hearing, which matters more than the pen.

lease5-wherein-shall-he-sleep.reason: Exodus 22:26-27 and its reasoning come first; the plain answer (a deposit is a pledge: held separately, returned on the clock, deductions itemised) arrives only past the midpoint.
lease5-wherein-shall-he-sleep.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Where does the deposit sleep at night? Somewhere set apart, because it is not yours. Yahweh let a lender take a pledge but not keep it overnight, since the poor man needed that cloak to sleep (Exodus 22:26-27). A security deposit is that kind of pledge, so it is held separately, returned on time, and every deduction is shown.
lease5-wherein-shall-he-sleep.example: THE CLOAK IN THE CUPBOARD. Say a landlord moves a tenant's $1,200 deposit into the operating account to cover a boiler. Nothing on paper changes, but the pledge has become a loan the tenant never agreed to make. If he has to wonder where that money is today, the cloak was kept overnight.
lease5-wherein-shall-he-sleep.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Where does the deposit sleep at night? In its own place, untouched, because it still belongs to the tenant. Hold it separately, so it never becomes a loan they did not agree to. Return it on the timetable the lease and the law set, without making them chase it. Itemise every deduction with a receipt. And before any fee, ask the question the passage asks: wherein shall he sleep? The One who hears that man's cry is gracious, which is good news for him and a warning to whoever holds the cloak.

teen.open: Where should a renter's deposit be kept? Somewhere separate, because it still belongs to them.
teen.close: So keep the deposit apart, give it back on time without being asked, and show a receipt for anything you take out. It's their money until they actually owe you.

senior.open: The title asks where a deposit should rest. Exodus 22 answers that a pledge may be taken but not kept from the one who needs it, and a deposit is a pledge.
senior.close: So the deposit sleeps apart from operating money, comes home on time, and leaves only with evidence for each deduction. Yahweh hears the one who cries, for He is gracious (Exodus 22:27).

lease6-every-man-under-his-own-vine.reason: Unpacks Micah 4:4 and fear as the measure first; the practical answer (notice, stated rent horizon, safe repair channel, early renewal, a known response time) arrives late, though the ending lands it.
lease6-every-man-under-his-own-vine.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Could your tenants actually sit down and rest? Only if nothing about you makes them afraid. Micah's picture of a household at rest includes the words none shall make them afraid (Micah 4:4), so fear, not mere legal compliance, is the test. A building can pass every inspection and still keep a family braced.
lease6-every-man-under-his-own-vine.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Could your tenants actually sit down and rest? They can when nothing about you is what they fear. So give written notice before entry as a stated policy, set a horizon for rent changes, keep a repair channel where asking never costs them, signal renewal early even when the answer is no, and keep a response standard they know. You cannot give a renter a vineyard or remove every uncertainty. You can remove yourself from their list of fears, and then you hold up your corner of the rest Yahweh has promised (Micah 4:4).

teen.open: Can your tenants really relax at home? Only if they are not afraid of you.
teen.close: So give notice before you come in, tell them about rent changes early, and make it safe to ask for repairs. You can't fix everything, but you can make sure you're not the thing they fear.

senior.open: The title asks whether tenants can truly rest. Micah's picture of rest includes freedom from fear (Micah 4:4), so fear is the honest measure, more demanding than compliance.
senior.close: So the test is whether anything about you makes them afraid. Clear notice, foreseeable rent, safe repair requests, early renewal word and known response times remove you from that list.

lease7-go-and-tell-him-between-thee-and-.reason: Matthew 18 and Galatians 6 are unpacked first; what the phone call actually does (finds the cause and the plan, and can gain the household) and the order to keep arrive late.
lease7-go-and-tell-him-between-thee-and-.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. What happens if you pick up the phone before you post the notice? You may gain the household instead of just a balance (Matthew 18:15). Most late rent has a cause, and a private call from a person tends to find the plan inside it. A notice on the door never has. Jesus put the private conversation first on purpose.
lease7-go-and-tell-him-between-thee-and-.example: THE CALL ON THE THIRD DAY. Say rent is three days late. Instead of a notice, you call. The tenant tells you the employer switched payroll and the check lands on the tenth. You agree on the tenth, note the call and its date, and the tenancy goes on. Had the notice gone first, both of you would now be defending positions.
lease7-go-and-tell-him-between-thee-and-.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. What happens if you pick up the phone before you post the notice? You often find the cause and the plan hiding inside it, and you may keep the household as well as the rent. So go first, alone, in meekness, considering yourself (Galatians 6:1). Record the call, add one more voice if it is refused, and only then run the formal process, the same day if your state requires it. The notice is not the sin. The notice instead of the visit is.

teen.open: What if a landlord called before posting a late-rent notice? Often they'd learn why the rent was late and find a fix together.
teen.close: So call first, kindly and privately. If that doesn't work, the formal steps can follow. Just don't skip the talk.

senior.open: The title asks what a phone call can do before a notice. Jesus' first step is a private word, and its aim is a person gained (Matthew 18:15).
senior.close: So call first, in meekness, and record that you did. Most late rent has a cause and a plan behind it, and only a conversation finds them. The formal step may follow; it must not come first.

lease8-as-much-as-lieth-in-you.reason: Romans 12:18 answers early (your half has no exemptions; the outcome is not yours); then reviews the course and ends on Galatians 6:9 weariness rather than restating the answer to the title.
lease8-as-much-as-lieth-in-you.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Can you keep the peace when the tenant lied, trashed the unit and sued? You can keep your half of it, and that is all Yahweh asks (Romans 12:18). Peace is sometimes not possible, and their choices are not yours to answer for. But their bad conduct never releases you from your own, because the verse says with all men.
lease8-as-much-as-lieth-in-you.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Can you keep the peace when the tenant lied, trashed the unit and sued? Your half, yes, every time. Return the call, state the number honestly, itemise and evidence the deduction, return the deposit on the clock, give full notice, and tell the next applicant the truth. Their choices, their story about you and the outcome do not lie in you, so stop weighing yourself on them. Every practice in this course works without the tenant's cooperation, and if you do not grow weary, the harvest comes in due season (Galatians 6:9).

teen.open: Can you stay at peace with a tenant who lied and caused damage? You can do your part, even if they don't do theirs.
teen.close: So keep doing your half: honest numbers, calls returned, deposits back on time. What they choose isn't on you. Don't get tired of doing right.

senior.open: The title asks whether peace is possible with a tenant who has wronged you. Romans 12:18 limits the outcome but not the scope: your portion is owed to all men.
senior.close: So your half remains fully in your hand, whatever they did, and the outcome is not yours to carry. The danger is weariness, and the promise of due season belongs to those who do not faint (Galatians 6:9).
